headline: The backup power was fine. It just never got the signal to start.

slides.html:
The backup power was fine. It just never got the signal to start.

What Google Cloud’s London outage teaches about failover you have never really tested.

20 Oct 2026 · europe-west2-b · London
07:00A cable fault cuts the zone’s main utility feed.+0The second feed is already offline for maintenance.+0Generators do not start.~5 minUPS batteries run out. Servers, storage and network lose power.~6 hUntil most services recover.

Times in UK time, from Google’s incident report.
One sensor, wired in the wrong place

Every part worked. The combination had never been tried.

Generators were tested. The feeds were maintained. The UPS did its job.

But the backup path had never run under the exact condition that triggers it: one feed already down, the other failing.

A failover you have not tested in that state is a hypothesis, not a plan.

Losing one zone stressed the other two

Workloads failed over from zone b to zones a and c at the same time. That demand surge, plus control-plane dependencies across zones, spread the impact wider than one building.

Ask of your own design:

→ Can the surviving zones absorb the full load?
→ Does anything you need to recover live only in the failed zone?

Test the failover you actually depend on

01

Test in degraded states. Fail the backup while maintenance is already in progress.

02

Check what the detector sees. Health checks can report “healthy” from the wrong vantage point.

03

Size for N−1. Remaining zones must carry peak load, not average load.

04

Map recovery dependencies. Your restore path must not need the thing that failed.

Remember this

Redundancy you have not exercised is an assumption.

The riskiest moment is during maintenance — when one safety net is already gone.

Plan for the failover load, not just the failure.

When did you last test failover while something else was already broken?

Tell me in the comments — honestly.
